Rudolf Gwalther
roo'dolf gval'ter
n. (Rudolf Gwalther, 1519–1586, Zwingli's son-in-law and Bullinger's successor as chief pastor of Zurich)
German Rudolf, famous wolf, from Germanic hrod and wulf; Gwalther, a Swiss form of Walter, ruler of the army.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Rudolf Gwalther was brought up in Bullinger's household after Kappel, married Zwingli's daughter Regula, and so stood by blood and by marriage at the centre of the Zurich church for sixty years. He studied at Basel, Strasbourg, Lausanne and Oxford, translated Zwingli's Latin works into German and his German works into Latin, and published the Archetypae homiliarum, complete sets of model homilies on the New Testament books that gave hard-pressed country pastors something sound to preach from. When Bullinger died in 1575 Gwalther succeeded him as antistes and held the office eleven years, keeping Zurich steady through the hardening of the Lutheran-Reformed division and corresponding with the English bishops and the persecuted of France. He was the third man in a single unbroken line — Zwingli, Bullinger, Gwalther — and his part was to hand on what the first two had built. “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” (Psa 145:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a homily as a sermon or discourse on a point of doctrine, and succession as a following in order, the act of taking another's place.

expand to see more

HOM'ILY, n. A discourse or sermon read or pronounced to an audience; a plain discourse on a point of doctrine.

SUCCES'SION, n. A following of things in order; the act of taking the place of another in office.

AN'TISTES, n. A presiding minister; in the Swiss churches, the chief pastor of a city.

DECLARE', v. To make known; to tell explicitly; to publish; to proclaim.

Modern Corruption

The third man of the Zurich line, who wrote homilies for country pastors.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suspicion attaching to printed sermon helps. Gwalther's homilies were written because many rural Zurich pastors had little Latin and no library, and the choice before them was a sound model or nothing. The abuse of such books by lazy men is real; it is not an argument against providing them for able men who are poor.

The principle to recover is that succession in the church is a succession in doctrine and labour rather than in office alone. Elisha asked for the thing itself and not the mantle only — “let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me” (2Ki 2:9) — and the promise made to Joshua as he took up Moses's work is the promise every successor needs: “as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee: I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee” (Jos 1:5).

Usage

"“One generation shall praise thy works to another” (Psa 145:4) — Zwingli, Bullinger, Gwalther."

"“as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee” (Jos 1:5) — succeeding to the Zurich pulpit in 1575."

"“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course” (2Ti 4:7) — sixty years in one city."
